BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r1.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r1.claim: His story says Decianus sealed the cave and later died; under the pious king Tindrous, whose people disputed bodily resurrection, God awakened the youths as proof.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r2.claim: Their long sleep, preservation from decay, and awakening demonstrate God's power and wisdom.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r3.claim: God awakened them so they would question one another, setting in motion the wisdoms that follow.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r4.claim: The questioner was their chief, whose name appears as Miksalmina; Bahr al-ʿUlūm records the form Maksalmina.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r5.claim: They guessed one day or part of one because they entered in the morning and woke late in the day, seeing the sun still above the horizon; this was a reasonable estimate, not a lie.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r6.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r6.claim: He says they entered in the morning and, seeing the sun near afternoon, guessed they had slept a day or part of one.

BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175#3/r7.claim: Al-Kashifi's account is more apt because sending someone with money required enough daylight for a round trip, unlike awakening just before sunset.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r1.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p176/r1.claim: Seeing their hair and nails grown, they told one another they had slept only part of a day.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r2.claim: They concede that only God knows the actual duration because it was immense and indeterminate to them, renewing the division into two groups.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r3.claim: They leave an irresolvable debate and send Yamlīkhā with silver; the demonstrative suggests a companion handed him the money for their day's food.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r4.claim: The coin may be minted or unminted; taking provisions is compatible with trust, because reliance follows ordinary means, as the Mathnawī teaches.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r5.speaker: مولانا
BURSEVI:v5p176/r5.claim: His couplet says that one who trusts should work and cultivate before relying on the Almighty; trust is no excuse for idleness.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r6.claim: The city was Tarsus, formerly called Ephesus; al-Qāmūs describes it as fertile and formerly Armenian before its return to Muslim rule.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r7.claim: The omitted noun in أيها is its inhabitants; أزكى means more lawful, wholesome, abundant, or inexpensive, and رزق is bodily sustenance.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r8.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p176/r8.claim: He says the city had people who concealed their faith, so the youths hoped to obtain meat slaughtered by believers.

BURSEVI:v5p176/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176/r9.claim: Let him act courteously to avoid being cheated or act discreetly so they are not recognized; an old count puts the Quran's midpoint at this word.

BURSEVI:v5p176#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p176#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p176#2/r1.claim: Not letting anyone sense their presence means avoiding acts that could lead to discovery, even unintentionally; the second reading reinforces careful conduct.

QASHANI:18:19/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19/r1.claim: Their raising is genuine spiritual awakening: they discuss latent meanings and realities of their capacities to actualize them; Sufis call this first awakening wakefulness.

QASHANI:18:19/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19/r2.claim: The question of their duration repeats an earlier interpretation; the correct group leaves it to God, then sends one with silver to the city for insight and completion.

QASHANI:18:19/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19/r3.claim: Silver signifies innate first principles that yield truths and divine knowledge; the city is a place of gathering or the city of knowledge, whose gate is ʿAlī.

QASHANI:18:19/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19/r4.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:18:19/r4.claim: A prophetic saying calls himself the city of knowledge and ʿAlī its gate.

QASHANI:18:19/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19/r5.claim: One envoy suffices because full perfection does not depend on everyone learning; the highest knowledge of one person can teach and awaken the rest.

QASHANI:18:19#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19#2/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19#2/r1.claim: The purest food means the city's best knowledge, free of excess, disputation, dialectic, grammar, and empty appearances that cannot strengthen the soul; knowledge nourishes the heart.

QASHANI:18:19#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19#2/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19#2/r2.claim: Be discerning and choose a verified pure-hearted, upright, complete guide, not a superficial pretender who claims to teach what he lacks; companionship yields insight.

QASHANI:18:19#2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:19#2/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:19#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, act discreetly so ignorant people do not learn their situation or faith; if the youths symbolize spiritual faculties, the envoy is thought, city their gathered faculties, and the best food intellect rather than illusion, imagination, or sensation.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r1.claim: They read بورقكم with kasra on rāʾ; Abu Amr, Hamza, and Abu Bakr from Asim use a quiescent rāʾ, and a report from Ruh describes assimilation.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r2.claim: Both ورق and ورق are regular vowel variants; assimilating qāf into kāf is good because qāf is farther back and the following kāf nearer the mouth, favoring this direction of assimilation.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r4.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r4.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r4.claim: The kasra form of ورقكم preserves its original vowel; sukūn avoids the succession of repeated kasras.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and ʿĀṣim pronounce the thāʾ distinctly in every occurrence of كم لبثت/لبثتم; the other four readers assimilate it.

QIRAAT-ER:18:19:29#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:19:29#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:19:29#1/r1.claim: Sukūn on rāʾ removes the short vowel between r and q in a dialectal variant.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r1.claim: Qatada glosses the best food as the finest food.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r2.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr interprets the best food as lawful food.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r3.speaker: عكرمة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r3.claim: Ikrima says it means more abundant food.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r17.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r17.claim: Warq means silver, whether minted or unminted.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p145#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p145#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p145#2/r1.claim: The two groups most likely are the youths themselves, as their later exchange shows; those saying the Lord knows best had realized the long duration, and the Quran first summarizes then retells the story at length.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r1.speaker: الزجاج والزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r1.claim: Al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī take the comparison in وكذلك to refer to God’s making the youths sleep: as He made them sleep, He raised them as a reminder of His power to cause death and resurrection, leading them to reflect, gain certainty, and give thanks.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r2.claim: The comparison echoes the earlier compressed account: God first made them sleep for counted years, then raised them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says كذلك refers broadly to what God did for them, while the lām in ليتساءلوا marks an outcome rather than the purpose of their awakening.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r4.claim: The questioner may have been their leader Miksalmina or the companion carrying their money, Tamlikha; كم asks how many days they had slept.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r5.claim: The respondents appear genuinely uncertain; أو may distribute the answers between them, one saying a day and another part of a day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r6.claim: One explanation says they slept at the day’s beginning and awoke near its end; their mistaken estimate follows their strongest impression and is not a lie, after which they defer the duration to God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says some youths corrected the others: evidence or divine inspiration had shown that the sleep lasted a long, indeterminate period known only to God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r8.claim: Their hunger after waking explains the shift to sending someone for food: they leave the duration question to God and attend to their immediate need.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r9.claim: Tamlikha was reportedly sent; the youths had brought coins for their expenses while fleeing, explaining their reference to these coins.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r10.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر والحسن والأعمش واليزيدي ويعقوب وخلف وأبو عبيد وابن سعدان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r10.claim: This group reads بورقكم with a still rāʾ; the other Seven and Zayd b. ʿAlī read its kasra.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r11.speaker: أبو رجاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r11.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads with kasra on wāw, a still rāʾ, and assimilation of qāf into kāf; Ibn Muḥayṣin is also reported with this assimilation, once with kasra rāʾ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r12.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p155/r12.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī attributes kasra rāʾ with qāf-kāf assimilation to Ibn Kathīr, but Abū Ḥayyān says this conflicts with the transmitters; al-Zajjāj reports kasra wāw and still rāʾ without assimilation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r1.claim: ʿAlī reads بوارقكم on the pattern فاعل as a collective noun like باقر and جائل.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r2.claim: The city was the youths’ hometown, said to be present-day Tarsus and called Ephesus when they left.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r3.claim: فلينظر may mean visual inspection or mental consideration; أيها may be an interrogative subject with an omitted predicate subject for أزكى, or a relative object under Sībawayh’s analysis.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r4.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAṭāʾ define أزكى as lawful slaughter and purer food, since most townspeople were unbelievers who sacrificed to idols.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r5.speaker: ابن جبير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r5.claim: Ibn Jubayr says أزكى means food that is lawful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r6.speaker: الضحاك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r6.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says much of the townspeople’s wealth came from unlawful seizure.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r7.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r7.claim: Mujāhid says they instructed the messenger not to buy food tainted by wrongdoing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r8.speaker: عكرمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r8.claim: ʿIkrima glosses أزكى as more plentiful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r9.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r9.claim: Qatāda glosses أزكى as better quality.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r10.speaker: ابن السائب ومقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r10.claim: Ibn al-Sāʾib and Muqātil gloss أزكى as tastier.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r11.speaker: يمان بن ريان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r11.claim: Yamān b. Rayyān glosses أزكى as cheaper.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r12.claim: Other glosses are more blessed or fruitful, or refer to rice, dates, or raisins; an omitted أهلها would make the phrase ask which town’s people had the purest food, otherwise it refers to implied foods.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r13.claim: Carrying provisions is presented as the practice of those who rely on God rather than depending on other people’s stores; one scholar says a pilgrim needs only a money belt and trust in the Merciful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r14.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r14.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says وليتلطف can mean taking care in the transaction to avoid being cheated, or being discreet in concealment; Abū Ḥayyān prefers concealment from the context.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r15.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r15.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads وليتلطف with kasra on the lām of command.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r16.speaker: قتيبة الميال
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r16.claim: Qutayba al-Mayyāl reads وليتلطف with a ḍamma yāʾ in the passive.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r17.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r17.claim: ولا يشعرن forbids conduct that unintentionally alerts anyone; it is called making them aware because it causes that awareness.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r18.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r18.speaker: أبو صالح ويزيد بن القعقاع وقتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p156/r18.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ, Yazīd b. al-Qaʿqāʿ, and Qutayba read ولا يشعرن بكم أحد in the active voice, with أحد raised as subject.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r1.claim: In إنهم, the pronoun may refer to the city’s unbelievers inferred from context, or to the generic أحد, which can take a plural pronoun as in 23:8.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says إنهم refers to the townspeople elided after أيها.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r3.claim: ظهور means discovering their location, though some take it as gaining ascendancy over them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r4.speaker: زيد بن علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r4.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī reads يظهروا with ḍamma yāʾ in a passive construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r5.claim: The threatened رجم is most likely stoning; the king intended to kill them, and stoning was an established punishment for dissenters in earlier times.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r6.speaker: حجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r6.claim: Ḥajjāj says رجم means verbal abuse, as Ibn Jubayr also reports.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r7.claim: يُعيدوكم إلى ملتهم means force you back into their religion; returning to something can mean becoming it even without prior membership.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p157/r8.claim: لن تفلحوا means you will not prosper if you enter their religion; إذا marks a conditional consequence.

SULAMI:v1p407#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r1.claim: A lover's time with the beloved feels short however long it lasts, because longing never reaches its end; its conclusion is another beginning.

SULAMI:v1p407#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r2.speaker: يوسف بن الحسين
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r2.claim: When buying food for poor people or people of spiritual knowledge, choose delicate food as the cave youths were told to be gentle; for ascetics and worshippers, buy whatever is available because they discipline their appetites.

SULAMI:v1p407#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r3.speaker: أبو عثمان المعزي
SULAMI:v1p407#2/r3.claim: Treat people of gnosis with gentleness and spiritual novices with firmness.

AKHFASH:v2p429/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v2p429/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v2p429/r2.claim: فلينظر does not govern أيها directly because النظر can be followed by a question, as in انظر أزيد أكرم أم عمرو.

FARRA:v2p137/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p137/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p137/r3.claim: Asim and al-A'mash read بورقكم lightly; it refers to silver, with dialectal vowel variants like كبد and كلمة.

FARRA:v2p137/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p137/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p137/r4.claim: أزكى طعاما is interpreted as meat from an animal slaughtered lawfully, since the sleepers' people were Magians.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r1.claim: God revived the sleepers from a slumber resembling death.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r2.claim: Wariq means silver, coined into dirhams or not; a report says ʿArfaja ibn Asʿad's silver nose became malodorous, so the Prophet ordered a gold one.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r3.claim: The report says the Prophet instructed ʿArfaja ibn Asʿad to replace his silver nose with gold.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r4.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r4.claim: Azka food can mean the greatest quantity, best quality, or lowest price; the root means growth and increase.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r5.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r5.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r5.claim: Lā yushʿiranna means “let no one know”; the root also appears in phrases about noticing, knowing, and the perceptiveness of a poet.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r1.claim: Their awakening is likened to their prolonged sleep; the correspondence is that both are signs of God's overwhelming power.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r2.claim: The purpose or consequence of awakening them was that they question one another, leading to the wisdoms narrated next; mentioning this effect also entails the other effects.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r3.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229/r3.claim: Al-Khafaji favors reading the lām as consequential: questioning was an outcome, since God's purpose was to display His power rather than to cause their discussion.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r1.claim: The dialogue's introductory قال is a resumption that explains how they questioned one another.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r2.claim: The questioner is identified either as their leader Maksalmina or as Yamlikha, who managed their provisions.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r3.claim: The questioner may have remarked on the unusual mismatch between their condition and what normally happens; another suggestion is that they were alarmed at missing prayer.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r4.speaker: غير واحد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r4.claim: They used aw for uncertainty because they could not establish how long they had slept; Alusi says sleep haze kept them from checking signs, whatever the time of sleep or waking.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r5.claim: The well-known account has them sleep in the morning and wake late in the day; another says they could not tell whether it was the same or next day.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r6.claim: One explanation takes aw as a correction: they first said a day, then noticed the sun had not set and corrected it to part of a day; Alusi maintains the straightforward reading is doubt.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r7.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r7.claim: Abu Hayyan reports a distributive reading: some said a day and others part of a day, each speaking from probable judgment; Alusi says this reading is unlikely and conjecture is unnecessary.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r8.claim: Their reply that God knows their stay best gently corrects the first group, displays proper etiquette, and marks the dialogue's two groups; the same speaker saying both is disfavored by the discourse structure.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r9.claim: The proposal that one person made both statements does not fit the passage's resumption and question-and-answer form.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r10.claim: Aḥadukum means one of you; using aḥad rather than wāḥid avoids a possible implication that they mean their chief.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r11.claim: Wariq is commonly explained as minted dirhams, though another view includes unminted silver; the Arfaja report about a silver nose that became foul supports the broader sense, while al-Asmaʿi's paper-leaf reading is dismissed because the report of silver rotting is unsound.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r12.claim: Reciters vary on wariqikum: many use a still rāʾ, Abu Rajaʾ and others use kasra on wāw with assimilation, a form with kasra on rāʾ is defended as rare Arabic, al-Zajjaj reports a non-assimilated form, and ʿAli reads bawariqikum as a collective noun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r13.claim: Calling the coin hadhihi suggests the speaker held it out; carrying provisions for livelihood is compatible with reliance on God, as the saying instructs one to tie the camel and trust.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r14.speaker: بعض الأجلة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p229#2/r14.claim: Some eminent scholars define the elect's trust as abandoning all causes, citing Khalid's drinking poison and reports of Saʿd, Abu Muslim, and Tamim facing extraordinary dangers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r1.speaker: أحمد، إسحق
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r1.claim: Ahmad, Ishaq, and other imams allow those strong in certainty and reliance to cross deserts without provisions and to forgo earning or medical treatment; Ahmad defines trust as ending dependence on people.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r2.speaker: إبراهيم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r2.claim: The account of Abraham refusing Gabriel's offer of help while being thrown into the fire illustrates reliance directly on God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r3.claim: The position that abandoning means of support is uniquely a Sufi doctrine is mistaken; it is also reported from others.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r4.claim: The city was their familiar home city, reportedly called Ephesus when they left and later Tarsus; this reconciles the two transmitted names.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r5.claim: Their immediate turn to obtaining food instead of investigating their situation exemplifies a wise redirection to what mattered then; the verse's fa also signals this.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says the people of the city sacrificed to idols; another report says they sacrificed pigs, so azka can mean lawful.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r7.speaker: الضحاك
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r7.claim: Al-Dahhak says most of the townspeople's wealth had been usurped, supporting a request for the purest lawful food.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r8.speaker: ابن السائب، مقاتل
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r8.claim: Ibn al-Saʾib and Muqatil explain azka as more wholesome or pleasant; if it means lawful, it returns to the preceding interpretation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r9.speaker: عكرمة، يمان بن ريان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r9.claim: ʿIkrima says azka means more plentiful, while Yaman b. Rayyan says cheaper.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r10.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r10.claim: Qatada interprets azka as best quality, which Alusi calls the best reading; it may also mean rice, dates, or raisins, though the youths are presumed to seek lawful food.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r11.claim: The increase implied by zakāh can be spiritual and otherworldly, as in the reward and good outcome of seeking lawful food, or material and worldly, as in abundance, affordability, or quality.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r12.claim: Ay may be an interrogative subject with azka as predicate, or a relative object with an elided predicate; its suffix can refer to the city, its people, or the food understood from context.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p230/r13.claim: The pronoun in rizqan minhu may refer to the best food or to the coins, making min partitive, source-marking, or a substitute marker; in either case the requested provision should be lawful.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r1.claim: The command to act gently means either to treat people tactfully so no quarrel exposes them, to hide their entry and exit, or to avoid being cheated; the next command warns not to let anyone in town notice them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r2.claim: On the concealment interpretations, wa-la-yushʿirannakum confirms and explains tact; the Imam takes it literally as do not inform anyone about you.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r3.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r3.claim: Al-Hasan reads the imperative lām in yatalattaf with kasra.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r4.speaker: قتيبة الميال
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r4.claim: Qutayba al-Mayyāl reads yutalattaf with a passive verb and ḍamma on yāʾ.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r5.speaker: قتيبة، أبو صالح، يزيد بن القعقاع
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r5.claim: They read yushʿirannakum as an active verb and aḥad as its nominative subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r6.speaker: ابن العربي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p231/r6.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi calls the passage the strongest proof for agency; al-Kiya also derives the permissibility of pooling group coins, jointly buying and sharing food, with an eater allowed extra money for his portion.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r3.claim: Their awakening means a return to sobriety after spiritual intoxication.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r4.claim: Their guess that they had slept a day or part of one reflects absorption that erased awareness of days and the distinction between moon and sun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r5.claim: The brief estimate also symbolizes lovers' tendency to count union as short: even a long meeting seems brief, and the cited poem says a life passed without counting nights.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r6.claim: Returning from intoxication to sobriety and spirituality to embodied life, they seek human food and apply spiritual principles to practical conduct.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r7.claim: The shared purse teaches aspirants not to beg, rebuking mendicant shaykhs who make a habit of asking, perhaps for unlawful money.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r8.claim: Calling it “your silver” teaches companions to share resources rather than reserve something for one member, even though one of the youths may have been a shepherd without money.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r9.speaker: ذو النون
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r9.claim: Seeking the purest food teaches scrupulousness; Dhū al-Nūn says a knower does not extinguish the light of gnosis with the light of scruple.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r10.claim: Al-Ālūsī criticizes a shaykh who accepted money certainly taken from an oppressor, claiming the money was like hot coals that cooled hungry seekers, despite the shrine and votive offerings later attached to him.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r11.claim: Gentle dealing with the food seller teaches good manners and kindness.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r12.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r12.claim: Some exegetes say the command means to select delicate food because they had not eaten and coarse food might harm their bodies; others say their spirits from the sacred realm suit only delicate things.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r13.speaker: يوسف بن الحسين
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r13.claim: Yūsuf ibn al-Ḥusayn says to buy delicate food for gnostics, while ascetics may eat whatever is found because they are still disciplining themselves; another view contrasts coarse diets of strivers with the gnostic's preference for delicacy.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r14.claim: Al-Ālūsī says making delicate food a rule impairs spiritual perfection; even if the report about ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī is true, it could be accidental or for a lawful reason, and it conflicts with reports of the Prophet and major Companions' simple diet and clothing.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r15.claim: Keeping the matter secret means concealing spiritual realities from people veiled from their light and insight.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r6.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r6.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r6.claim: Baʿathnāhum means We brought them back to life, from the language of resurrection.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r7.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r7.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r7.claim: Azka ṭaʿāman means more abundant food; the verse comparing seven tribes with three attests this.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r8.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r8.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r8.claim: Lā yushʿiranna means let no one know about you; shaʿartu means I knew it, hence the word poet.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r1.claim: As God preserved their bodies from decay during their long sleep, He raised them from a sleep resembling death; asking questions was an outcome, not the purpose of raising them.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r2.claim: Maksalmina, their leader, asked how long they had slept; they were startled and may have worried that they missed prayer.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r3.claim: They entered in the morning, awoke near evening, first estimated a day, then revised that to part of a day when they saw sunlight remained.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p159/r4.claim: Their long hair and nails finally convinced them they had slept longer than a day.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r1.claim: The group said God knew best how long they had remained; one account says their leader ended their disagreement.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r2.claim: They sent Yamliḫā with their silver; wariq means silver whether coined or uncoined.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r3.claim: They read wariq with a still rāʾ; the others use kasra, with the same meaning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r4.claim: The city is identified as Tarsus, whose pre-Islamic name was Ephesus.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r5.claim: Azka is interpreted as lawful food, especially meat slaughtered by a believer rather than for another deity, since some believers concealed their faith.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r6.speaker: الضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r6.claim: He interprets azka as tastier food.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r7.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r7.claim: He interprets azka as the best-quality food.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r8.speaker: عكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160/r8.claim: He interprets azka as more abundant food.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p160#2/r1.claim: The envoy is to bring back food as provision, act discreetly on the road and in town, and keep anyone from learning where the sleepers are.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r1.claim: Their awakening is a second sign of God's power, teaching them about resurrection and prompting gratitude and certainty.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r2.claim: Thinking they had slept a day or part of one reflects a sleeper's inability to measure time; alternatively, they entered in the morning and awoke at noon, then reconsidered after seeing their hair and nails.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r3.claim: The line saying their Lord knows best may be one party correcting the others, or an objection by the others to their estimate.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r4.claim: Their silver waraqa may be coined or uncoined; variant readings lighten, double, or assimilate its consonants, and taking food shows that trusting God still permits provision.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r5.claim: The city is Tarsus; azka food means lawful and tasty, or more abundant and cheaper.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:19/r6.claim: The messenger should deal gently to avoid being cheated or act discreetly to avoid recognition, and must do nothing that alerts anyone.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p451/r1.claim: ‘Thus We raised them’ means We woke them, and ‘so they might ask one another’ means each would ask the others.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p451/r2.claim: Libtum is an allowed assimilated form because the two articulation points are close.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
NAHHAS:v2p451/r3.claim: Reporting from Ibn Abbas, he says one youth estimated a day and another about a day; their leader warned that disagreement brings ruin.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r4.speaker: أهل المدينة
NAHHAS:v2p451/r4.claim: They assimilate the final bāʾ in ‘with your silver’; Ibn Kathir also assimilates qāf into kāf.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r5.speaker: أهل الكوفة وأبو عمرو
NAHHAS:v2p451/r5.claim: They omit the kasra in ‘with your silver’ because it is heavy.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r6.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v2p451/r6.claim: He records a form with kasra on wāw, like kibid and fakhidh.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r7.speaker: نحوي غير مسمى
NAHHAS:v2p451/r7.claim: Another grammarian says silver can be called riqqa, from warqa with its initial wāw deleted.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r8.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p451/r8.claim: ‘Which one is purer’ means which town’s people or food; the phrase has an understood ‘people.’

NAHHAS:v2p451/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v2p451/r9.claim: As reported by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, the youths sought the cleanest food because the townspeople slaughtered pigs.

NAHHAS:v2p451/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p451/r10.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p451/r10.claim: The lām in li-yaʾtikum and li-yatalaṭṭaf may be read with kasra, its original vowel.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r6.claim: Their revival and questions deepen their faith and certainty by revealing God's comprehensive knowledge and power, answering deniers of resurrection.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r7.claim: The story answers Quraysh's consultation with Jewish questioners: either the Jews' admission should lead both to faith, or their denial shows signs cannot guide everyone.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r1.claim: The questioner sensed a long sleep from the sleepers' appearance or other indications; their answer of a day or part was only conjecture.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r2.claim: God's acceptance of their mistaken estimate shows that reasoned conjecture is permissible and is not a lie merely because it misses the fact.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r3.claim: They end the disagreement by entrusting the hidden duration to God, and their agreement reflects affection and fellowship in faith.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r4.claim: They send one of their group with their silver money to their former city, Tarsus, to find the purest and best food.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r5.claim: The envoy must act tactfully and avoid alerting anyone, including through unintended actions that reveal the group.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r6.claim: Their conduct shows that a traveler may carry provisions while relying on God, and the account supports the validity of agency.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p454/r7.claim: The author derives الورق and its related forms from a root associated with gathering, explaining silver coins by their shape, beauty, and role in a person's livelihood.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r1.claim: The lexical family includes foliage, worldly beauty, paper, animal life, fallen blood, and wealth; these senses are tied to beauty, life, and the gathering of human affairs.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r2.claim: Waraq can mean a group's beauty or its young and weak men; الورقة may mean either a lowly or noble person depending on which aspect is considered.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p455/r3.claim: Related forms describe both failure and prosperity: a hunter or group may return fruitless, while الأورقوا can also mean gaining much wealth.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r1.claim: The extended lexicon gives varied meanings for foliage and verdure, early pasture, a variegated wolf, and a flaw in a bow, linking these to color, usefulness, or lack of fruit.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r2.claim: Related q-w-r forms describe walking on tiptoe or stalking prey, carving circular openings, compact hills and rocks, spacious houses, and states of gathering or contraction.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p456/r3.claim: The author connects these senses through gathering, separation, or cutting, and cites the proverb قد أنصف القارة من رماها for the tribe called Qara.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r1.claim: After the first tyrant died, a just king who worshipped God ruled; the sleepers awoke and differed over whether they had slept one day, two days, or longer.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r2.claim: Their leader warned that disagreement destroys peoples, then sent one of them to town with their old coin to buy food discreetly.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r3.claim: The old coin and the youth's unfamiliarity with the current king alerted a baker and governor; the youth's answers drew a crowd and led them to a scholar.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r4.claim: A scholar found the names in the old tablet and told the people that God had led them to their long-lost brethren.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r8.claim: The king prayed for a sign to settle disagreement over resurrection: some affirmed body and soul together, while others said the soul rises and the body is eaten by the earth.

DURR-FULL:v5p366/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r9.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v5p366/r9.claim: God raised the sleepers as the sign; one was sent to buy food and found that faith had become public in the city.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas says أزكى طعاما means meat lawfully slaughtered, since people there sacrificed to idols.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas also glosses أزكى as purer, since people there slaughtered pigs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r1.claim: The Cave and Dhul-Qarnayn stories are the surah's primary purposes, placed at its beginning and end.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r2.claim: The surah's placement near the Qur'an's midpoint is a divinely inspired arrangement: one proposed midpoint letter is ت in وليتلطف (Q 18:19), another is ن in نكرا (Q 18:74), and the midpoint of its thirty parts is at Q 18:75.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r1.claim: The revival benefits the sleepers themselves: it lets them see God’s protection and gives them direct knowledge of one aspect of resurrection, as Abraham asked about reviving the dead.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r2.claim: Kadhālika may compare awakening with the preceding sleep as an equally powerful sign, or compare the revival with itself to heighten wonder, as at 2:143.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r3.claim: The statement ‘they questioned one another’ is explained by the ensuing dialogue: a questioner asks how long they slept and the others answer.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r4.claim: Those answering ‘a day or part of a day’ may have agreed together, or the wording may distribute the answers, with some saying a day and others part of one.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r5.claim: After disagreeing, all apparently defer the duration to God; it may instead be one speaker’s answer collectively attributed because the others judged it correct.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p283#2/r6.claim: Rather than continue debating the duration, they send someone for food, a ‘wise style’ that redirects the questioners to their more immediate need.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r1.claim: Wariq means silver; the common reading has a kasra on rāʾ, while several readers use sukūn, and it refers to a minted silver coin or dirham.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r2.claim: An unnamed report says their coins were dirhams from the Roman ruler Decius; the city is Ephesus, identified earlier in the story.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r3.claim: Ayyahā means which place within the city, such as a market stall; azkā food is the purest or best, with ṭaʿāman specifying the comparative relation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r4.claim: Azka means better and more wholesome because zakā conveys increase in goodness and benefit; rizq means provision, as at 12:37.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r5.claim: The commands may address an unspecified delegate, or a known companion omitted in the narration; either way, the group must instruct him to return with food and act discreetly.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r6.claim: A saying counts the tāʾ in walyatalaṭṭaf as half of the Qur’an’s letters; Ibn ʿAṭiyya instead records the nūn in nakran at 18:74 as the midpoint.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p285/r7.claim: Ishʿār means informing; its causative hamza derives from shaʿara, which can mean knowing, and the verb here takes one object.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r1.claim: The phrase means ‘do not inform anyone that you exist’; an omitted noun lets the warning cover every circumstance, including their number and location.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p286/r2.claim: The emphatic nūn warns of consequences; the threat in the following clause explains both the prohibition and its emphasis.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r1.claim: 'Likewise' points to God's preceding treatment of the youths; baʿth means setting something in motion after stillness, and the lam in 'so they might question one another' marks an outcome rather than their purpose.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r2.claim: The question about duration suggests that a speaker sensed their sleep had exceeded ordinary limits; they seem to have awakened under similar time and weather conditions, since an abrupt change would be unlikely.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r3.claim: Readers vary between warq with kasra or sukūn on rāʾ; other reported forms change the vowels or assimilate consonants, while Ali reads bawāriq, a collective noun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r4.claim: Narratives say they awoke hungry and sent Tamlikha to buy food after praying as though only one night had passed; the cave entrance may have collapsed or a shepherd may have opened it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r5.claim: In the extended story, Tamlikha put on shabby clothes, found the city and its landmarks changed, saw signs of the Christian faith, and feared that he had lost his mind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505/r6.claim: He tried to buy food with an old coin; the seller and townspeople recognized it as money from an ancient king and questioned him about a hidden treasure.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r2.claim: Ibn Atiyya says he has shortened the many conflicting versions, retaining the details needed to explain the verse and relying on what he considers sounder.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r3.claim: The youths' use of an agent to buy food establishes the validity of agency; Ali appointed his brother Aqil to act for him in Uthman's presence.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r4.claim: Most readers use a silent lām in the command falyanzur; al-Hasan pronounces it with kasra.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r5.claim: Ikrima glosses azka as greater in quantity; Qatada says better, Muqatil says more pleasant, and Ibn Jubayr says lawful, especially in view of food slaughtered by unbelievers.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r6.claim: The author explains the lawful interpretation in light of food slaughtered by unbelievers; the youths are reported to have sought raisins, or dates in another account.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p505#2/r7.claim: Liyatalattaf means to act discreetly and carefully; al-Hasan reads the lām with kasra.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r1.claim: As with their earlier sleep, God raised them so they would ask and dispute about the duration, offering a lesson to observers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r2.claim: They entered in the morning and woke at day's end, so first guessed one day, then revised this to part of a day after seeing the sun.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r3.claim: He identifies the speaker who returned the question to God's knowledge as Yamlīkha, their leader.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r4.claim: In another report, Ibn Abbas names Miksalmina, the eldest, as the speaker.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r5.speaker: أبو سليمان
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r5.claim: This disagreement suggests they sensed they had stayed longer than their first estimate.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r6.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r6.claim: Another explanation for their uncertainty is that they saw how long their nails and hair had grown.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r7.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r7.claim: أحدكم means one person from among them; واحدكم might imply a distinguished or honored one.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r8.claim: ورق means silver, whether coined into dirhams or not; the report that ʿUrfaja fashioned a silver nose supports this sense.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r9.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r9.claim: They read بورقكم with a light rāʾ carrying kasra.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r10.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r10.claim: They read بورقكم with a still rāʾ; Abu Amr's reading is assimilated with slight emphasis.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r11.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r11.claim: The city they left is called Daqsus; some say its present name is Tarsus.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r12.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r12.claim: Azka food means slaughtered meat lawful to eat; most people in the city were idolaters who sacrificed to idols, though some concealed their faith.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r13.speaker: سعيد بن جبير والضحاك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r13.claim: A second view makes azka mean lawful food; al-Dahhak says much local property had been seized unjustly.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r14.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r14.claim: Mujahid says they told their companion to avoid food tainted by injustice or usurpation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r15.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r15.speaker: عكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r15.claim: A third interpretation is that azka means more plentiful.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r16.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r16.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r16.claim: A fourth interpretation is better or higher quality.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r19.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r19.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p120/r19.claim: The root zakā means growth and increase.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p122/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p122/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p122/r1.claim: They ask for food to eat, tell the messenger to inspect carefully and act discreetly, and forbid him from revealing their location.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r1.speaker: الزجاج والزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r1.claim: كذلك means “as we put them to sleep, so we awakened them”; that refers to the sleeping act, making awakening another sign.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r2.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r2.claim: Ibn Atiyya takes ليتساءلوا as eventual result because awakening was not intended for questioning; the author prefers causal purpose.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r3.claim: كم is adverbial with “days” omitted, supplied by the answer.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r4.claim: أو in أو بعض يوم may express uncertainty or distribute the answers among different speakers.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r5.claim: بورقكم is circumstantial to أحدكم, meaning he goes accompanied by or carrying it.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r6.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and Abu Bakr use fatḥa waw with silent ra; the others use the original kasra, while sukun is easing.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r7.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj transmits kasra waw with silent ra, comparing vowel variants like كبد.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r8.speaker: أبو رجاء وابن محيصن
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r8.claim: They also read it this way but assimilate قاف; critics object to two adjoining sukun letters. Ibn Muhaysin is also reported to assimilate ra's kasra.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r9.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r9.claim: A reading بوارقكم means “the possessor of silver”; ورق may also be a collective noun.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r10.claim: ورق means coined silver or silver generally; الرقة omits its first فاء; hadith says it owes one quarter of a tenth.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r11.claim: أي in أيها أزكى may be interrogative or relative; أهلها is understood and طعاما is a tamyiz.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r12.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19/r12.claim: Alternatively there is no ellipsis: its pronoun refers to foods understood in context.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r1.claim: Most readers use sukun on command-lām in وليتلطف; al-Hasan uses the original kasra.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r2.claim: Qutayba al-Mayyāl reads وليتلطف in the passive.

SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو صالح وقتيبة
SAMIN-DURR:18:19#2/r3.claim: They read ولا يشعرن with open ياء and damma عين; أحد is the subject.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r1.claim: After 309 years, God raised the youths with their bodies, hair, and skin unchanged.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r2.claim: They guessed they had slept a day or part of one because they entered early in the day and awoke late, then admitted God knew best how long it was.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r3.claim: They turned to their more urgent need for food and drink and sent one of their number with their silver coins to the city from which they had departed.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145/r4.claim: They had brought coins from home for their needs and spent some, leaving the remaining silver to take to their city.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r1.claim: Azka taaman most likely means tastiest or purest food, supported by 24:21 and 87:14 and the root sense of purifying; another view takes it as more abundant, as a poetic line suggests, but the youths sought lawful wholesome food regardless of quantity.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p145#2/r2.claim: Let him be discreet in going, shopping, and returning; do not let anyone know about you.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r1.claim: They read بورقكم with a still rāʾ; the other readers kasra it, and Abū ʿAmr also assimilates qāf into kāf. The variants retain the same meaning: silver, coined or uncoined.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r2.claim: Baʿth originally means stirring something up and also means sending messengers or raising the dead.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r3.claim: Zakā can mean growth or purity, as in the verse about purifying them.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r4.claim: Luṭf can mean smallness, gentleness in an action, or God's kindness and mercy.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r6.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r6.claim: The likeness in ‘thus We raised them’ compares raising them from sleep to preserving them during their long sleep; either act exceeds anyone's power but God's.

JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r7.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v6p4377#2/r7.claim: He says they were raised in exactly the condition in which they had fallen asleep, with nothing changed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r1.claim: Their awakening, like their sleep, displays God’s power over both sleep and resurrection, prompts inquiry, reflection and certainty, and calls for gratitude.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r2.claim: Their estimate of a day or part of one rests on predominant conjecture; this permits ijtihad and probable judgment, which may be mistaken without being a lie.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r3.claim: Some correct the others: the duration was long, known only to God, perhaps inferred from evidence or divine inspiration.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r4.speaker: رُوي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r4.claim: They entered the cave in the morning and awoke after noon, first supposing it was still the same day; their long nails and hair prompted their estimate.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r5.claim: Their turn to sending someone for food means they stop debating an unknowable duration and attend to a more urgent need.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r6.claim: Wariq means silver, whether minted or unminted.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r7.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r7.claim: A report says ʿArfaja lost his nose at the battle of al-Kulab, tried a silver replacement that smelled, and was ordered to use gold.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r8.claim: Wariq is read with the ra still or moving; Ibn Kathir has kasra on ra and assimilates qaf into kaf.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r9.speaker: ابن محيصن
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r9.claim: Ibn Muhaysin reads waw with kasra, ra still, and assimilation; al-Zamakhshari rejects it as an impermissible meeting of two still letters.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r11.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r11.claim: Their carrying travel provisions and money exemplifies the prudent reliance of those who trust God, rather than relying on chance or others’ stores.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r12.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r12.claim: Aisha told someone asking about a pilgrim in ihram fastening his money belt to secure his provisions.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r13.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r13.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r13.claim: He recounts an ascetic scholar who declined wealthy townspeople’s offers to finance pilgrimage, saying travel requires a money belt and trust in the Merciful.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r14.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r14.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r14.claim: “Among them” means among the city’s people, with “people” elided as in the command to ask the town.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r15.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r15.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r15.claim: Azka food may mean most lawful, pleasant, abundant, or inexpensive.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r16.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r16.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r16.claim: “Be tactful” may mean taking care in the purchase to avoid being cheated, or keeping discreet so no one recognizes the envoy.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r17.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r17.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r17.claim: The warning not to let anyone know includes avoiding actions that unintentionally cause people to notice them; the wording calls that causing awareness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r18.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r18.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p663/r18.claim: The pronoun in “they” refers to the implied people of the city in “among them.”

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r1.claim: Their being raised means that they were awakened; God also put their dog to sleep with them, according to Muqatil.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r2.claim: They asked each other how long they had slept so they could determine its duration.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r3.claim: One youth guessed they had slept a day because that was the longest familiar sleep; seeing the sun still up, he revised it to part of a day, since they had slept early and awakened late.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r4.claim: ربكم أعلم بما لبثتم may be God's statement that He knows the length of their stay.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r5.claim: Alternatively, the eldest youth Maksalmina ended the disagreement by saying that their Lord knows how long they stayed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r6.claim: The word ورق is read with either a kasra or a silent rāʾ, and in both readings means silver coins; ورق with a fatḥa means camels or sheep.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r7.claim: A poem uses ورقي for a person's camels and sheep, supporting the livestock sense with fatḥa.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r8.speaker: عكرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r8.claim: أزكى طعاما may mean the greatest quantity of food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r9.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r9.claim: أزكى طعاما may mean the most lawful food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r10.speaker: الكلبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r10.claim: أزكى طعاما may mean the tastiest food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r11.claim: A further interpretation takes أزكى طعاما to mean the cheapest food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r12.claim: فليأتكم برزق منه may mean bringing food for them to eat.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r13.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r13.claim: Alternatively, it means bringing food lawful for them to eat.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r14.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r14.claim: وليتلطف may mean bargaining carefully for a low price.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r15.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r15.claim: Alternatively, it means being discreet about their situation.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r16.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r16.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p293/r16.claim: The instruction supports sharing food and pooled costs among a group, a practice called munāhada that pre-Islamic Arabs disapproved of but Islamic law permits.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r6.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r6.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r6.claim: God awakens them to question one another; Maksalmina, the oldest, asks how long they have slept.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r7.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r7.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r7.claim: They guess one day or part of a day because they entered the cave in the morning and awoke near the day's end.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r8.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r8.claim: Maksalmina alone tells them their Lord knows their duration better, returning the matter to God.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r9.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r9.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r9.claim: Maksalmina proposes sending one of them to town with their coins; they send Yamliha.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r10.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r10.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r10.claim: Azka food means the tastiest food; the messenger should act discreetly so no one notices or learns their whereabouts.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r1.claim: As God made them sleep, He awakened them too, displaying His power over both sleep and resurrection.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r2.claim: Their questioning helps them learn what happened, reflect on God's power, increase certainty, and give thanks for His favor.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r3.claim: The questioner was their leader, who asked how long they had stayed.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r4.claim: Their answer of a day or part of one rests on predominant conjecture and shows that reasoning and acting on such conjecture are permissible.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r5.claim: Some answered that God knew best after signs or inspiration showed them the stay had been long and its exact duration was known only to Him.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r6.claim: A report says they entered in the morning and woke after noon, then judged from their long nails and hair that the sleep had lasted a long time.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās inferred that the sleepers were seven from the singular questioner, the plural answer, and a further plural reply.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r8.claim: One of them was sent, namely Tamlīkha; wariq is silver, whether coined or uncoined, and several readers pronounce its rāʾ still.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r9.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r9.claim: The city is Tarsus; taking provisions for travel is proper for those who trust God, unlike relying on chance or empty claims of reliance.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r10.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r10.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r10.claim: Some scholars, longing for the Sacred House, said travel requires only packed provisions and trust in the Merciful.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r11.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r11.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r11.claim: In “which of them,” the أهلها is elided, as in “ask the town”; azkā can mean more lawful, wholesome, plentiful, or cheaper.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r12.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r12.claim: Ṭaʿāman is a specification (tamyīz), and the envoy should obtain provisions from the food he finds.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r13.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r13.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r13.claim: He should act gently in the purchase so he is not cheated, or remain discreet so no one recognizes him.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r14.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r14.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p7/r14.claim: The envoy must not cause anyone to discover them, even unintentionally; the source calls him the cause of their being noticed.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r1.claim: Baʿath means movement from stillness; here God awakened the youths in the same clothes and condition as before sleep.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r2.speaker: شاعر
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r2.claim: An unnamed poet uses baʿath for waking young men at dawn.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r3.claim: The lām in li-yatasaʾalu is a consequence lām, not a purpose: their awakening resulted in their questioning, as in 28:8.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r4.claim: They entered the cave in the morning and awoke late in the day; their leader, called Tamlikha or Maksalmina, said God knew the duration.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas compares their silver currency to the hooves of a young camel.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r6.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r6.claim: These readers pronounce the rāʾ in waraqikum with kasra; other readers make it still, and both are dialects.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r7.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r7.claim: They read waraqikum with a still rāʾ, removing the kasra as heavy; al-Zajjaj records a form with kasra on wāw.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r8.speaker: الغزنوي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r8.claim: The youths awoke hungry, and al-Ghaznawi identifies the dispatched youth Tamlikha as the youngest.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r9.claim: The city was Ephesus, also called Tarsus; its earlier name was Ephesus and it was renamed Tarsus after Islam. Ibn Abbas says their coins bore the current king's image.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas says their silver coins carried the image of the king of their time.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r11.claim: Azka food means meat slaughtered lawfully because townspeople sacrificed in the name of idols; Ibn Abbas also says most inhabitants were Magians.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r12.claim: Other readings of azka are more blessed, tastier, or cheaper; they may have asked for enough food for several people, with rice, raisins, or dates proposed.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20/r13.claim: Rizqan means food; let the delegate act discreetly in town and tell nobody, lest discovery expose the rest of the youths.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r1.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عوف
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r1.claim: A Bukhari report says Abd al-Rahman contracted with Umayya ibn Khalaf to protect each other's dependents in Mecca and Medina; Umayya objected to the name al-Rahman.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r2.speaker: الأصمعي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r2.claim: Al-Asmaʿi explains saghiya as a man's adherents who incline toward him, from the verb meaning to incline.
