QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r3.claim: Agency is a delegated contract allowed because people need help managing affairs and not everyone can handle every task alone.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r4.claim: Jurists support agency from this verse, 9:60, 12:93, and many hadiths, including the report of Urwa al-Bariqi.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r5.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r5.claim: Jabir says he was sent to Khaybar and told by the Prophet to collect fifteen wasqs from his agent, using a hand on the collarbone as proof if asked.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r6.claim: Agency is valid in any right that can be delegated, but not for a usurper or an unlawful act.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r7.claim: Agency in this story arose from fear of discovery; scholars agree that people with an excuse may appoint agents, while most permit healthy present people too.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r8.speaker: أبو حنيفة وسحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#2/r8.claim: Abu Hanifa and Sahnun disallow agency for a person present without an excuse; Ibn al-Arabi speculates Sahnun used this against oppressors, while al-Qurtubi permits it for virtuous people.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r1.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r1.claim: In Abu Hurayra's report, the Prophet repaid a camel debt with a better camel, and the creditor praised him; the Prophet said the best people pay best.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r2.claim: This sound report shows a healthy person present may appoint others: the Prophet authorized his Companions to repay for him, contrary to Abu Hanifa and Sahnun.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r3.speaker: ابن خويز منداد
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r3.claim: Ibn Khuwayz says the verse supports partnership because the youths shared their money, agency because they sent a buyer, and joint eating despite unequal appetites.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r4.claim: The school allows a poor person to mix donated food with a rich person's meal and a business agent to mix provisions and eat together.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r5.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r5.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says the verse does not prove shared partnership because each youth may have given money separately; he relies instead on two hadiths.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r6.speaker: ابن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r6.claim: Ibn Umar cites the prohibition on taking two dates together without a companion's permission as evidence about shared food.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#3/r7.claim: The army-of-khabt report is less decisive because Abu Ubayda may simply have distributed equal portions rather than having everyone share one supply.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:19-20#4/r1.claim: The permission to mix with orphans as siblings and the permission to eat together or separately support shared eating; the source cites 2:220 and labels the latter 24:16.

ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r1.claim: Wariq has four vowel patterns, with kasra on wāw the least acceptable; qāf may assimilate into kāf.

ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r2.claim: أيها is nominative as a topic meaning which inhabitants of the city; أزكى is its predicate and طعاما a specification.

ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r3.claim: أزكى طعاما may mean lawful food, since most townspeople were Magians who did not properly slaughter animals, or food not obtained unlawfully.

ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r4.claim: A second interpretation is food not taken by usurpation or from an illicit source.

ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r1.claim: In فليأتكم, the lām is read with sukūn; kasra is permitted.

ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r2.claim: ولا يشعرن بكم means let no one know of you; if the messenger is discovered, he should not expose his companions to danger.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r1.claim: Their awakening was like revival from sleep resembling death; they had remained alive without food or drink, and were turned over, so God revived them to question one another about their stay.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r2.claim: Their questioning can itself be an intended purpose: it disclosed extraordinary aspects of God's power, and such disclosure is desirable for its own sake.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r3.speaker: المفسرون
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r3.claim: Commentators say they entered the cave in the morning and awoke near day's end, explaining why they guessed a day or part of one.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the speaker who returned the duration to God as their leader Yamlikhā, who inferred from their changed hair, nails, and faces that much time had passed.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read wariqikum with sukūn on rāʾ and fatḥa on wāw; Ibn Kathīr reads kasra on rāʾ and assimilates qāf into kāf.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r6.speaker: ابن محيصن
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r6.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin's reading combines kasra on wāw with sukūn on rāʾ and assimilation, which Rāzī rejects because it creates two consecutive sukūns.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r7.claim: Wariq means silver, coined or uncoined; a report about ʿArfaja using a silver nose supports the uncoined sense, and several vowel forms are attested.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r8.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ lists the forms waraqu, warqu, and wariqu, and calls kasra on wāw the least good form.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r9.speaker: الأزهري
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r9.claim: Al-Azharī says riqqa, another word for silver, derives from wariq through the pattern of ṣila and ʿida.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r10.speaker: المفسرون
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r10.claim: Commentators say the youths carried coins bearing the image of the king of their time and that their city was what is now called Tarsus.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r11.claim: The episode shows that taking steps to secure food is important and does not negate reliance on God.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r12.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the purest food as lawful slaughter, since most inhabitants were Magians, though some secretly believed.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r13.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r13.claim: Mujāhid says they sought food farthest from the tyrant's injustice; other glosses understand the phrase as tastiest or cheapest.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r14.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r14.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses ayyuhā as subject, azkā as its predicate, and ṭaʿāman as a specification.

RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r15.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r15.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p87/r15.claim: The emissary should act discreetly while entering the city and buying food, and tell nobody where the youths are.

ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r1.speaker: most commentators
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r1.claim: Most commentators take li in li-yatasa'alu to express purpose: so that the youths might ask one another.

ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n23/r2.claim: Asad instead reads li as lam al-aqibah, marking causal sequence, which he renders as and they began to ask.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.claim: The youths awoke after a shepherd opened the cave while seeking shelter for his flock from rain.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r2.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r2.claim: Some say they estimated a day because they entered the cave in the morning and awoke at sunset.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r3.speaker: R, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r3.claim: Others say they noticed their long hair and nails before concluding that God knew best how long they had slept.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r4.claim: Their one-day estimate resembles the man awakened after a hundred years and Quranic accounts of people thinking their wait before resurrection was short.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r5.claim: The parallel reactions connect the Cave story symbolically with death, resurrection, and the intervening barzakh.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r6.claim: The chosen youth carried a silver dirham stamped with the oppressive king’s image and was told to buy food discreetly to avoid persecution.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.claim: The old coin exposed the youth; centuries had passed and the city was ruled by the righteous king Tīdhusīs, or Theodocius.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.claim: When the youth rejoined the others, they returned to deep sleep; the king and townspeople later found their bodies perfectly preserved.

ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r1.claim: The matching question and answer in 2:259 link both allegories to God's power to create life, end it, and resurrect.

ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n24/r2.claim: The story also exposes the deceptive, earthbound human conception of time.

ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n25/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n25/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:19#n25/r1.claim: Some sleepers understood that the interval had no independent reality, as with death and resurrection; this explains the two viewpoints in verse 12.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r5.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r5.claim: The youths sent one of their number to Ephesus with an old coin; the townspeople recognized its age, consulted the king and records, and rejoiced when they learned the youths' story.

TAB-FULL:v15p196/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p196/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p196/r1.claim: The youths question one another because they find their long sleep strange; some estimate a day or part of one, believing that is how long they slept.

TAB-FULL:v15p196/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p196/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p196/r2.claim: The others defer the matter to God, saying that their Lord knows best how long they remained asleep.

TAB-FULL:v15p197/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r1.claim: The youths send one of their number to their former city, Ephesus, to buy food because they have awakened hungry.

TAB-FULL:v15p197/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r2.claim: Wahb says a shepherd opened the cave for sheltering sheep from rain; the youths revived the next morning and sent one with old silver to buy food, revealing their long sleep to a righteous king.

TAB-FULL:v15p197/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v15p197/r3.claim: When the messenger led the king and people to the cave, terror kept them from entering; they later built a church or mosque there for prayer.

TAB-FULL:v15p199/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r1.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r1.claim: Ikrima reports that Christian youths, sons of Roman kings, withdrew from their people and slept until a Muslim community and king arose, then sought God's sign amid a dispute about bodily resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v15p199/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r2.claim: The awakened envoy's old coin exposed the era he came from, and the king presented the youths as a sign that body and soul are resurrected together.

TAB-FULL:v15p199/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r3.claim: Qatada says that when people entered the cave they found bodies without souls, and the king called them a sign from God.

TAB-FULL:v15p199/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v15p199/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas, passing the cave on campaign with Habib ibn Maslama, says the youths' bones had already vanished more than three hundred years later.

TAB-FULL:v15p200/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r1.claim: Ibn Ishaq's account places the awakening under the righteous king Theodosius, whose reign lasted sixty-eight years and whose people split over belief in the Hour.

TAB-FULL:v15p200/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r2.claim: The disputants included believers and deniers who claimed only souls, not bodies, would be raised and forgot scripture; falsehood gained ground over the believers.

TAB-FULL:v15p200/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r3.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r3.claim: Theodosius withdraws, wears sackcloth, sits on ashes, and prays in grief for a sign to resolve the dispute.

TAB-FULL:v15p200/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r4.claim: God intends the youths' appearance to establish the Hour and bodily resurrection as truth, answer Theodosius' prayer, preserve his faith and rule, and gather dispersed believers.

TAB-FULL:v15p200/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p200/r5.claim: God inspires Olyas to remove the stones from the cave entrance for a sheep pen; terror keeps people at a distance while the youths sit up revived, greet each other, and pray unchanged.

TAB-FULL:v15p202/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r1.claim: After prayer, the youths ask Yemliha what happened and estimate their sleep as a day or part of one; he says Deqianus seeks them and will force sacrifice or kill them.

TAB-FULL:v15p202/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r2.speaker: مكسلمينا
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r2.claim: Maksalimina urges them to face death without abandoning belief in God or the life after death.

TAB-FULL:v15p202/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r3.claim: They instruct Yemliha to go secretly to town, learn what is said about them, and bring more food; he takes their old coins and sees the cave entrance has been unsealed.

TAB-FULL:v15p202/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p202/r4.claim: The youths think they have slept only their usual night and still believe Deqianus is seeking them, unaware that 309 years have passed.

TAB-FULL:v15p203/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r1.claim: Yemliha sees Christian signs displayed at the city gates and hears people openly invoking Jesus, unlike the persecution he remembers; the changed city leaves him bewildered.

TAB-FULL:v15p203/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r2.claim: He asks a local youth the city's name and learns it is Ephesus, yet fears he has lost his mind and tries to leave unseen.

TAB-FULL:v15p203/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p203/r3.claim: When Yemliha offers an ancient coin for food, sellers pass it around and suspect he has found a buried treasure from long ago.

TAB-FULL:v15p204/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r1.claim: The townspeople accuse Yemliha of hiding a treasure, threaten to take him to the ruler, bind him, and parade him through the streets as a stranger.

TAB-FULL:v15p204/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r2.claim: They bring him to the city's two righteous governors, Arius and Astius; he believes he is being taken to Deqianus and cries to God for help.

TAB-FULL:v15p204/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p204/r3.claim: Yemliha fears separation from his brothers and recalls their pledge never to forsake faith or one another in life or death.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r1.claim: The city they fled was Ephesus, and the youths woke from their long sleep hungry, so they asked for food.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r2.claim: When Yamlīkha returned with the old coin, two city officials suspected he had found a treasure; he said it was his fathers’ currency and could not explain his situation.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r3.claim: No one recognized Yamlīkha or his father; some called him mad, while the officials accused him of lying and threatened torture until he confessed.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r4.claim: Asked about Daqyanus, the townspeople said no such man lived and that the king had died long ago; Yamlīkha realized centuries had passed.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r5.claim: Yamlīkha said he had seen Daqyanus enter Ephesus the previous evening, asked the officials to see his companions, and Areus recognized a possible sign from God.

TAB-FULL:v15p206/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p206/r6.claim: Areus, Astius, and the townspeople, both prominent and ordinary, accompanied Yamlīkha toward the cave to see the sleepers.

TAB-FULL:v15p208/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p208/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p208/r1.claim: When Yamlīkha delayed, his companions feared Daqyanus had captured him; hearing horses, they prayed, exchanged farewells, and expected to face the tyrant.

TAB-FULL:v15p208/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p208/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p208/r2.claim: They found Areus and the townspeople at the cave instead; Yamlīkha told the youths what happened, and they understood God had awakened them as a sign of resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v15p211/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r1.claim: The youths were raised under a Muslim king, hungry; one judged they had slept a day or less, then deferred the true duration to God and went to buy food with old coins.

TAB-FULL:v15p211/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r2.claim: The old coins dated from a king three hundred and nine years earlier; the merchant took Yamlīkha to the Muslim king, and the account matched an archived tablet.

TAB-FULL:v15p211/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r5.claim: Medinan and some Iraqi readers pronounce ورقكم with fatḥa on wāw and kasra on rāʾ; most Kufan and Basran readers make rāʾ quiescent.

TAB-FULL:v15p211/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r6.claim: Some Meccan readers kasrate rāʾ and assimilate qāf into kāf; all readings carry the same meaning and reflect known Arabic forms.

TAB-FULL:v15p211/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r7.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p211/r7.claim: The original form is ورق with wāw fatḥa and rāʾ and qāf kasra, so al-Ṭabarī prefers that reading while accepting the others as sound forms of Arabic.

TAB-FULL:v15p212/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p212/r1.speaker: مقاتل
TAB-FULL:v15p212/r1.claim: A report transmitted from Muqātil identifies the youth sent with the coins as Yamlīkh.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r1.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r1.claim: ʿIkrima interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which resident has the most food.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r2.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which food is more lawful.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r3.claim: Qatāda gives the sense as asking which food is better.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r4.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers lawful and pure food: requiring the best makes sense whether a seller has much or little, and lawful good food outweighs abundant unlawful food.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r5.claim: The more-food interpretation draws on Arabic usage where zakā can mean increase; an unnamed poem uses أزكى to mean more, but al-Ṭabarī says that does not decide the verse’s sense.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r6.claim: أيها is grammatically attached to the city but means its inhabitants, since listeners understand that the food belongs to people.

TAB-FULL:v15p213/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r7.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p213/r7.claim: The youths may have meant which food was lawful because they had left an idolatrous people and would not permit themselves to eat their sacrificial meat.

TAB-FULL:v15p214/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p214/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p214/r1.claim: رزق means food or sustenance to eat.

TAB-FULL:v15p214/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p214/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p214/r2.claim: The messenger should act gently and cautiously while shopping, traveling, and entering the city, and ensure no one learns about the youths.

TABATABAI:18:23/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:23/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:23/r4.claim: The cave sleepers mirror humanity absorbed in earthly adornment: people will awaken from worldly life and reckon its long span as a day or part of one.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r1.claim: Tasāʾul is mutual questioning; waraq is dirhams or silver, coined or uncoined; yuẓhirū ʿalaykum can mean discover or overcome you.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r2.claim: “Likewise We awakened them” refers back to their long, remarkable sleep; the questioning was the immediate purpose of waking them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r3.claim: Their despair at the apparent triumph of coercive falsehood parallels the man revived after a century; their awakening shows that time's length does not destroy truth or revive falsehood.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r4.claim: Earthly life and its events pass like a brief dream, but worldly distraction keeps people from recognizing the truth until death or the end of the world.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r5.speaker: علي عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r5.claim: Ali says people are asleep and awaken when they die.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#10/r6.claim: Humanity will also awaken when the world's adornment is folded up and the human world is brought to extinction.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r1.claim: The questioning is the real purpose of awakening and aligns with the purpose stated in 18:12.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r2.claim: Treating the questioning as only a subordinate purpose lacks textual evidence; treating it as a mere consequence does not answer the objection that it is a small outcome of a great miracle.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r3.claim: One youth asked the others how long they had slept, apparently sensing a long interval from the heaviness of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#11/r4.claim: “A day or part of a day” is one speaker's uncertain estimate based on the sun's changed position, not a division in which some said a day and others part of one.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r1.claim: Observed sun, shadows, light, and darkness cannot establish an exact full day; here “day” commonly means slightly more than a night and day.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r2.claim: Saying “your Lord knows” states an epistemic truth: humans know external events only through indicators, while God alone directly encompasses each thing and event.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r3.claim: The speakers who appeal to God's knowledge show higher monotheistic insight than those who estimate a day; they are a different group, not the factions in 18:12.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r4.claim: The dialogue implies at least seven youths: one asks, and each of two plural replies requires at least three people.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r5.claim: They propose sending one of their own to buy food; “which one” refers grammatically to the city but means its residents.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#12/r6.claim: The requested errand is to obtain food for them to eat, introduced as a proposal to the group.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r1.claim: Zakiy food may mean good, lawful, or pure food; the comparative form favors the first sense.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r2.claim: In “bring you sustenance from it,” the pronoun most naturally refers to the food; taking it to refer to the silver is remote and requires an extra implied pronoun.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r3.claim: Talaṭṭuf is acting gently and showing care; in context the envoy should deal smoothly with residents to avoid a quarrel that reveals them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r4.claim: A broader reading of tact as general caution in transactions is not supported by the explicit following clause.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r5.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r5.claim: Al-Rāghib traces ẓuhūr to visibility, from which the word extends to learning of something, finding it, or prevailing over it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r6.claim: The author prefers “discover your location” for yuẓhirū ʿalaykum because it covers how the powerful townspeople could then capture and overpower the youths.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r7.claim: The choice of stoning signals the townspeople's hostility to the youths' faith and the likelihood of a collective attack.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r8.claim: “Return you into their creed” uses a verb carrying the sense of insertion, hence the preposition fi rather than ilā.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#13/r9.claim: Being returned would likely mean enforced participation in idol worship and loss of their true religious practices, not only verbal assent.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r1.claim: A captive or weak person trapped in an unbelieving society may comply under coercion while keeping faith inwardly, as 16:106 and 3:28 allow.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r2.claim: Someone free to leave who voluntarily enters a hostile society and loses the ability to profess faith has wronged himself; 4:97 rebukes those who claim they were helpless despite a spacious earth.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r3.claim: The author rejects proposed harmonizations: coerced apostasy leading to Satanic influence, return by invitation alone, or a period when dissimulation was forbidden lack textual support.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#14/r4.claim: The exchange portrays close fellowship: they share religious insight, delegate equally, use communal money, advise tact, and care for one another's safety.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r1.claim: The emphatic phrase “your silver, this” is unusual for a food errand; the coin's age—three centuries—caused the youths to be recognized.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r3.claim: They entered the cave with the dog and slept until that king and city disappeared, then awoke in a new era and initially thought they had slept a day or part of one.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r4.claim: One youth went for food with old currency, found a changed city and mutually unintelligible people, and was questioned after asking for provisions.

TABATABAI:18:26#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r3.claim: A report from Abu Jaʿfar says the youths were money changers.

TABATABAI:18:26#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r4.claim: Al-Sadiq distinguishes money changers in speech from dealers in coins.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r2.claim: A later just king’s era began before God awakened them; they disputed whether they slept a day or longer, then sent one with an old coin to buy food, exposing the changed city and era.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.claim: The coin seller alerted officials, who identified the youths from the tablet; the messenger entered the cave while the crowd could not find or enter it, and they built a mosque to pray and seek forgiveness for them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r3.claim: The report’s claim that some said two days or more conflicts with the Quran’s day or part of a day and with ordinary evidence; differing about duration is a disagreement in judgment, not blameworthy dissent in action.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.claim: The Qurʾānic narrative first shows the youths’ truth-bearing withdrawal and long sleep, then their awakening and exchange that exposes them, and finally their discovery and the mosque built over them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.claim: After 309 years God raised the youths to show how He had rescued them; they awoke disoriented, and some guessed they had slept a day or part of one while others deferred to God’s knowledge.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r2.claim: Because they were hungry, the youths sent one with their silver to find wholesome food and instructed him to act discreetly, fearing stoning or forced return to their religion.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.claim: God allowed their discovery after the persecuting generation and its rule had passed; the new population, dominated by monotheists and disputing resurrection, would receive a sign of it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.claim: The messenger expected the same city, but its people and conditions had changed over three centuries; his old silver exposed him as one of the vanished youths, and the news brought the townspeople to the cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r1.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Abū Bakr, Ḥamza, and Khalaf read warq with a silent rāʾ, while the others use kasra; Abū ʿAmr and Abū Rajāʾ are reported with k-q assimilation, though Ibn Jinnī calls it concealment rather than true assimilation.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r2.speaker: ابن جني
TABRISI:18:19-20/r2.claim: Ibn Jinnī says the k-q sequence is concealed rather than assimilated; true assimilation would transfer the qāf’s kasra to rāʾ, and readers sometimes call concealment assimilation for convenience.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r3.claim: ‘How long did you stay?’ means ‘how many days did you stay?’ with the counted unit omitted; kam is accusative as the object of labithtum.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r4.claim: The clause ‘which food is purer/better’ is the object of ‘let him look,’ and ṭaʿāman is a specification.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r5.claim: God woke them as He had preserved them for so long, producing an event that resembled resurrection.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r6.claim: Their discussion of how long they had slept prompts recognition of their Creator and strengthens their certainty.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r7.claim: Commentators say they entered the cave in the morning and awoke near sunset, so they first guessed a day and then said perhaps part of a day when they saw the sun.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:19-20/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Tamlikhā, their leader, was the one who returned the matter to God by saying their Lord knew how long they had remained.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:19-20/r9.claim: The silver coin was a dirham bearing the image of the ruler of their time; the city was the one they had left.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:19-20/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the best food as the cleanest and lawfully slaughtered because most city residents were Magians, though some believers hid their faith.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r11.speaker: الكلبي
TABRISI:18:19-20/r11.claim: Al-Kalbī interprets azkā as tastier food.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r12.speaker: عكرمة
TABRISI:18:19-20/r12.claim: ʿIkrima takes azkā as more plentiful, from the idea that wealth grows; the best food would be found where there was more of it.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r13.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r13.claim: Alternatively, the city sold food that the youths considered impermissible.

TABRISI:18:19-20/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:19-20/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:19-20/r14.claim: The envoy should bring back some food and act discreetly; alternatively, he should shop gently without haggling or arguing with the seller.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p151#2/r3.claim: The youths wake joyful, pray as before, and still think Daqyanus is pursuing them; they ask Tamlikha what happened the prior evening.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p151#2/r4.claim: They suppose they slept a day or part of one, while Tamlikha says the city searched for them and the tyrant plans to sacrifice or kill them.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r5.speaker: مكسلمينا
THALABI:v6p151#2/r5.claim: Maksalmina warns his companions that they will meet God and must not renounce their faith if summoned the next day.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p151#2/r6.claim: They send Tamlikha to learn the news and buy more food discreetly, since their earlier supply was too small.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p151#2/r7.claim: Tamlikha carries old coins bearing Daqyanus's stamp and notices stones removed from the cave entrance, but does not know the tyrant died 300 years earlier.

THALABI:v6p152/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p152/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p152/r1.claim: Tamlikha sees Christian signs over the gates and hears people openly invoke Jesus, unlike the persecution he remembers from the previous evening.

THALABI:v6p152/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p152/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p152/r2.claim: He concludes the city may not be the one he knew; its name is Daphsus, and he fears he has lost his reason.

THALABI:v6p152/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p152/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p152/r3.claim: Merchants pass his ancient coins from hand to hand and suspect he has found an old treasure, then threaten to take him before the authorities.

THALABI:v6p153/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p153/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p153/r1.claim: The crowd binds Tamlikha and says he is unknown in the city; he waits for his family, certain they lived there the previous evening.

THALABI:v6p153/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p153/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p153/r2.claim: The crowd takes him to the two city leaders, the righteous Armos and Astius; he mistakes them for Daqyanus and prays for patience and support.

THALABI:v6p153/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p153/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p153/r3.claim: Tamlikha grieves that he is separated from companions with whom he had pledged never to renounce God, worship idols, or part in life or death.

THALABI:v6p154/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p154/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p154/r1.claim: The city leaders think Tamlikha's coin is from a treasure because its stamp is more than 300 years old, and threaten torture unless he confesses.

THALABI:v6p154/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p154/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p154/r2.claim: Tamlikha explains that Daqyanus forced them toward idol worship and asks the leaders to accompany him to the cave; Armos recognizes a possible divine sign.

THALABI:v6p155/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p155/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p155/r1.claim: The youths hear the approaching crowd and fear Daqyanus has come for them; they pray, then meet the returning Tamlikha with Armos and the townspeople.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p156#2/r1.claim: A report says Muhammad asks God to let him see the sleepers; God instead directs him to send four eminent companions to convey his message and invite them to believe.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r2.speaker: جبريل
THALABI:v6p156#2/r2.claim: Gabriel instructs Muhammad to seat Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Abu Dharr on the corners of a cloth and summon Solomon's gentle wind.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p156#2/r3.claim: The wind carries the four companions to the cave; the dog welcomes them, and God restores the youths' souls when they greet them.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r4.speaker: أصحاب الكهف
THALABI:v6p156#2/r4.claim: The youths return the greeting, accept Muhammad's message and Islam, and send him their greetings before resuming their sleep until the end time.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p156#2/r5.claim: A variant says the Mahdi will greet the youths, God will revive them, and they will sleep again until resurrection.

THALABI:v6p156#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p156#2/r6.speaker: أصحاب النبي
THALABI:v6p156#2/r6.claim: When Muhammad asks what happened, the companions report that the youths answered his greeting, accepted his prophethood, and praised God for sending him.

THALABI:v6p157/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p157/r1.speaker: رسول الله
THALABI:v6p157/r1.claim: The Prophet prays not to be separated from his in-laws, loved ones, family, and companions, and asks forgiveness for those who love him and his household.

THALABI:v6p161/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r6.claim: As God preserved their bodies and clothes from decay through the long sleep, He awakens them so they can talk and question one another.

THALABI:v6p161/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r7.claim: Maksalmina, their leader, asks how long they slept because the duration seems strange; another explanation is that they missed a prayer.

THALABI:v6p161/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r8.claim: They say a day or part of one because they entered in the morning, saw some sun remaining, and wished not to claim more than they knew.

THALABI:v6p161/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r9.claim: Seeing that their hair and nails had grown, they realize the sleep lasted longer and say their Lord knows best; another account has their leader end the disagreement this way.

THALABI:v6p161/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r10.claim: Waraq means silver, whether struck into coins or unminted; the author cites the Prophetic instruction that a companion replace a festering silver nose with gold.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وخلف
THALABI:v6p161#2/r1.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and Khalaf read the phrase with bi-wariqikum.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r2.speaker: أهل مكة
THALABI:v6p161#2/r2.claim: Meccan readers use wariqikum with a still ra and assimilated qaf.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r3.speaker: أكثر القراء
THALABI:v6p161#2/r3.claim: Most readers pronounce the opening waw with fatHa and the ra with kasra in bi-wariqikum.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161#2/r4.claim: The word waraq has variant vocalizations analogous to the cited forms of kabid and kalima.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161#2/r5.claim: The city they are sent to is Ephesus.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v6p161#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr interpret azka food as meat slaughtered lawfully, since most townspeople were Magians and some believers hid their faith.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r8.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
THALABI:v6p161#2/r8.claim: Muqatil ibn Hayyan glosses azka as better quality.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r9.speaker: يمان بن رئاب
THALABI:v6p161#2/r9.claim: Yaman ibn Ri'ab offers the gloss arfaḍ for azka.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r11.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v6p161#2/r11.claim: Ikrima glosses azka as more plentiful.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161#2/r12.claim: The root of zakat means increase and growth; a poem says seven tribes are more azka and better than three.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161#2/r13.claim: Rizq here means sustenance and food; talaṭṭuf means being discreet and gentle while shopping, traveling, and entering the city.

THALABI:v6p161#2/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161#2/r14.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161#2/r14.claim: The warning not to let anyone know means that if Tamlikha is discovered, he should not expose his companions to the same danger.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r1.claim: Thus points back to God putting them to sleep, increasing their guidance, and turning them over; just as God did those things, He raised them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r2.speaker: ابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565/r2.claim: He describes their bodies as emerging from that sleep, which resembled death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r1.speaker: أبو علي الجرجاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r1.claim: The purpose was for the youths to question one another and disagree about how long they had stayed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r2.claim: He takes the question to mean how long it had been since they entered the cave.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r3.claim: They entered in the morning and woke late in the day, first estimating a day and then revising to part of a day after seeing the sun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r4.claim: He says their leader Tamlikha returned knowledge of their duration to God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r5.claim: Warq means silver whether or not it has been struck into coins; the report about Arfaja making a silver nose supports the broader sense.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r6.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r6.claim: They record several vocalized forms of warq, with kasra on the first syllable the least preferred; silver may also be called riqqa.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r7.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r7.claim: He derives riqqa from wariqa, as ṣila and ʿida are derived forms.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r8.claim: The youths carried coins stamped with the image of the king from whose rule they had fled.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p565#2/r9.claim: The city was called Daqsus and is said to be the present-day Tarsus.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r1.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r1.claim: He interprets the best food as lawful slaughter; Saʿid ibn Jubayr agrees, and al-Farra prefers this because many townspeople were Zoroastrians while some believers hid their faith.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r2.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r2.claim: He says they sought the most lawful food because a tyrannical ruler oppressed people in food and markets; the messenger was told not to buy anything obtained by injustice or extortion.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r3.claim: He includes both explanations: the food was lawful either because it came from a believer slaughter or because it was free of theft; grammatically ayyu is subject, azka predicate, and taʿāman specification.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p567/r4.claim: He glosses walyatalattaf as acting in secrecy while entering the city and buying food; the word also means to inspect carefully and use a discreet plan.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r1.claim: He says the messenger must tell no city resident either about the youths or their location.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r2.claim: He interprets the warning as telling the messenger not to expose his companions if he himself is discovered.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r3.speaker: السدي وغيره
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r3.claim: They say the envoy was bound by an oath that, if captured, he would lead the captors to the others rather than keep the martyrdom to himself; the author finds this more fitting than Abu Ishaq reading.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p568/r4.claim: He prefers Ibn Abbas meaning: the envoy should not voluntarily inform anyone, but if discovered should point the discoverer to his companions so they share the testimony.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r1.claim: God awakened the youths from sleep resembling death so they would ask one another how long they had remained asleep.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r2.claim: They entered in the morning and were awakened late in the day; seeing the remaining daylight, they guessed it had been a day or part of one, while Temlikha deferred knowledge to God.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r3.claim: They sent one of their number with their silver coins to buy lawful food, either from a believer's slaughter or because it was not stolen.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:19-21/r4.claim: The shopper must act discreetly when entering town and buying food so no one learns their whereabouts.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r3.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r3.claim: They entered the cave early in the day; seeing a little sunlight remaining made them guess that they had slept a day or part of one, then they deferred the answer to God.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r4.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r4.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r4.claim: One youth is sent to town with their dirhams to buy food.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r1.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr says the best food is the lawful food; Yaḥyā notes that some foods of their people were not lawful to them, while another view takes it to mean the tastiest food.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r2.claim: The messenger should act subtly and keep their presence secret; discovery could lead to stoning or forced return to disbelief, after which they would never prosper.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r1.claim: Their awakening, like a sign of resurrection, first served to let them understand their own condition; knowing one's state is among the foremost concerns.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r2.claim: Some estimated one day and others part of a day; people raised at resurrection will likewise make such an estimate, as in the passage about the passerby in 2:259.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r3.claim: When some sensed they had slept longer, they ended the disagreement by acknowledging that their Lord knew the duration.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r4.claim: They sent one companion with their silver coin to find the cleanest food and bring provisions, acting carefully and keeping their presence secret.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r1.claim: Awakening the youths after a long fast without bodily decay exemplifies and proves that God can resurrect people after death.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r2.claim: The youths disputed how long they had slept and, unaware of elapsed centuries and changes in the world, thought their persecutors’ threat remained current.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r3.claim: They sent one companion into town for food and warned him to act carefully.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r4.claim: The messenger was exposed by his ancient clothes, coin, and speech, which differed from the people of his time.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r5.speaker: rivayetler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:19/r5.claim: Reports say the coin bore King Decius’s image; townspeople took the youth to the ruler, who was a monotheist Christian after Christianity had spread, then went with him to verify the story at the cave.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: God woke them so two groups would debate how long they slept; their guesses proved unreliable, foreshadowing how people in Barzakh will perceive their span as brief.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Just as God protected them, He awakened them so their mutual questioning would expose their inability to know the elapsed time; this expands the earlier summary.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Their mistaken sense of having slept briefly illustrates that after death in Barzakh and upon resurrection people will think their sleep lasted only a short time.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: “Pure food” means halal food: the youths fled a society unconcerned with lawful food and therefore instructed their companion to scrutinize what he bought.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Islahi allows that People of the Book may have lived in Raqim and been sensitive about food, but careful shopping could expose the youths.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Yatalattaf means carrying out a task cautiously, cleverly, and circumspectly.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Wariq literally means silver and may refer to coins or other forms of money; Islahi uses the broader translation “currency.”

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The verse leaves the exact discovery route unspecified; after investigation, people gradually learned the cave-dwellers' origins, possibly through the market trip.

QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r10.claim: The youths underestimated their long stay because they were absorbed away from themselves and lacked detailed awareness of their condition.

QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r11.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r11.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p213/r11.claim: He quotes a poem about an uncertain long night, then says days of union feel short however long they actually are; another poem compares morning and evening sweetness.

QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r1.claim: God knows how long they stayed because He is the one who placed them in that state.

QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r2.claim: While absorbed, they had no desire for food, drink, or bodily needs; upon returning to discernment, eating was their first concern, showing food's priority in human constitution.

QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r3.claim: The instruction to act gently includes dealing courteously with the person from whom food is bought.

QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p214/r4.claim: People of spiritual knowledge prefer subtle clothing and fine food, whereas practitioners of ascetic discipline accept coarse dress and food.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r3.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r3.claim: Abū Rajāʾ's بورقكم with kasra on wāw is hidden articulation of the qāf's kasra, not idghām; full assimilation would transfer the vowel to rāʾ, and connected-word examples argue for concealment.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r4.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r4.speaker: أبو حاتم
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r4.claim: Abū Ḥātim reports that Ibn Muḥayṣin actually read بورقكم with assimilation; Ibn Jinnī accepts that such assimilation is permissible.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p388/r5.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p388/r5.speaker: author
IBNMUJAHID:v1p388/r5.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ kasra rāʾ in bi-wariqikum; Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and Abū Bakr quiesce it. A report describes Abū ʿAmr's form as assimilated.
